result.title: Are Fake Citations a Form of Reward Hacking? A Pre-Registered Study of Post-Training and Citation Cues
result.comment: 49 pages, 3 figures, 20 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking (archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23845528)
result.summary: Post-trained language models fabricate citations at high rates. We ask whether that is reward hacking: scoring well on a proxy for scholarship while doing worse on what it stands for. We ran four pre-registered experiments on 900 frozen questions (US federal case law, computationally adjacent scientific literature, and medical literature) across twelve open-weights checkpoints covering four post-training stages of three model families, then refit on fifteen. The clearest result holds the weights fixed and changes only the prompt. Asking for citations raises fabrication sharply in post-trained checkpoints and not in base ones: a 47.8-point interaction on twelve checkpoints (Holm-adjusted p = 2e-34) and 41.5 points on fifteen, in all three domains. A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking

AI.brief_summary: 论文用四项预注册实验，在 900 个冻结问题、三个领域和 12–15 个开源 checkpoint 上考察后训练阶段与「要求给出引用」这一提示线索对伪造引用率的影响，并用只依赖表面引用特征的偏好模型检验奖励是否偏向引用数量。
AI.relevance_reason: 与视觉或多模态推理无直接关系，但其「表面特征充当代理奖励、指标看似变好而实质变差」的设定，可供核查 LVR 中评价与贡献分配是否被显式步骤、回答长度等表面线索误导。
